title: Cuban music after the revolution
summary: He discusses new Cuban groups, government control and Orquesta Aragon's change.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Not so much the Mozambique. Mozambique is more like an oldtime conga, street conga. But they got the oopa-oopa, they got the -- another one they got, they're recording now, they're calling -- I don't know, they got a whole lot of different names. And when I hear them, I say, this isn't Cuba, it's different countries.

But the joke is, they developed dancing into the other thing. Now they tell me, when you go up to one of the big dances, in Cuba, you play (unintelligible). The kids listen to him, applaud one number. They rather to hear the (unin-
telligible) play, they go out of their minds. Why? Because they were born with the _______.
And they apply the dancing to the _______ music. And the _______ music ain't all what you call (unintelligible) music.
Can you talk about _______ a little, and what _______ has done with the music?
Well, I tell you exactly what _______ is. The _______ is mental, mental, they're jazz-oriented. That's the formation of the group.

And I had a conversation with some of the -- in the middle of the streets. There was too much jazz-oriented. So somebody got into the _______ and said listen, let's get into the Cuban _______. So Valdez -- Chucho and the other Valdez, got no relation to him but a relation to (unintelligible) Valdez. (Unintelligible). We got to do something with the guitar, can sing something, to break the impact. And then we go to the other thing.

So right now, right now, inside our orchestra, there's two different _______. Well, almost one _______ the other. Because you take the Santo Bal and the Turo, and the alto player, they played (inaudible) this side of the river. The other side is the Cuban side. In the middle of all that,
(inaudible). Chucho made every side (unintelligible). How long that's going to survive, nobody knows.

The way I look at it, (unintelligible) has to survive. Because the government dictate there what you do. Nobody can get away from that, and we all know that. The governor dictate the culture, they tell you what you eat, what you work, there's no question about that. That's the system. That's the way the system is built. From the best to the worst. That's what it is.

But that is it right now in the group. I will listen to the last half of their release, I won't hear in America today, with a new label called __________. I think the company distributes (unintelligible) or something. And I had the first record. (Unintelligible.) So they tell me (unintelligible), and I know why. I had always a great orchestra. But (unintelligible). That was put away. Then they were playing __________ music until last year. You could not touch __________ music in Cuba until last year.

So the people, 18, 17, 18, don't like nothing about that music. Now, I listen to the Aragon music. So Aragon tried to bend himself to play the different rhythms, where they call them the (unintelligible), I don't know, a whole lot of different names. And I would listen to this record this morning, I got all I want, because you release it here.

And I said to myself, what is this? They could not play what they're supposed to. They way they play, the way I know they be capable to play, because this new thing -- they did that in order to satisfy whatever they had to satisfy. But I know (unintelligible). We've got to have good (unintelligible). And they sound to me like any third-rate orchestra. And I'm sorry if I hurt anybody when I say it. But that's my own opinion of what I heard.
